# Review Report — Reviewer 2 (R2): Novelty and Related Work

**Paper**: OntoCoDec: Near-Complete Type-Valid Information Extraction via Compiled Ontology Constraints

---

## 1. Summary

This paper identifies that LLM-based IE systems produce systematic ontology constraint violations (15-19% domain/range violation rates), proposes OntoCoDec—a two-layer constrained decoding framework combining grammar-level (XGrammar CFG) and semantic-level (stateful entity registry with dynamic logit masking) enforcement—and demonstrates 94% DR reduction on SciERC at zero F1 cost and 46% on DocRED. The paper also introduces a constraint tightness metric that correlates with residual violation rates (Spearman rho=0.52), providing practitioners with a priori estimates of enforcement effectiveness.

---

## 2. Strengths

- **Well-motivated problem with empirical grounding.** The violation landscape study (Section 3) is a genuine contribution. The finding that violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size (SciERC 15.4% with 7 relations vs. DocRED 18.7% with 96 relations) is non-obvious and useful. The per-relation breakdown (Table 5, Figure in Section 3) showing 42.4% for Compare vs. 0.8% for Used-for is compelling.

- **Honest and well-calibrated claims.** The title change from "Guaranteed" to "Near-Complete" reflects intellectual honesty. The paper proactively discloses the CF violation trade-off (0.08% to 9.9%), identifies its root cause (per-relation independent enforcement + type system ambiguity), and correctly frames it as an open challenge rather than sweeping it aside.

- **Clean ablation design.** The five-way ablation (Table 3/scierc-ablation) with unconstrained/grammar-only/semantic-only/full-S1/full-S2 cleanly decomposes contributions. The enabling dependency observation—semantic-only achieves only 24% DR reduction vs. 94% with grammar enabled—is well-demonstrated and provides architectural insight beyond mere additive composition.

- **Thorough related work.** Section 6 covers five distinct paradigms (grammar-constrained decoding, semantic constrained decoding for code, vocabulary/type-constrained generation, structural constraints via training/prompting, post-hoc ontology validation, quality concerns) with appropriate differentiation. The positioning relative to type-constrained code generation (Synchromesh, MGD, PLDI 2025) is particularly well done—the paper correctly identifies the mechanistic analog and articulates the genuine differences (flat domain/range sets vs. deep subtype hierarchies; free-text span type inference vs. declared type annotations).

- **The prompt insufficiency finding is valuable.** The Evaluate-for regression (24.1% to 29.9% with schema-informed prompting) is a concrete demonstration that prompt-level intervention can be counterproductive, strengthening the motivation for decoding-time enforcement.

- **Cross-model generalization evidence.** Llama-3.1-8B achieving 92% DR reduction with cross-model per-relation Spearman rho=0.89 is meaningful, though limited to SciERC.

---

## 3. Weaknesses

- **The core technical contribution is thin.** Stripped to its essentials, the grammar layer is a direct application of XGrammar with a JSON schema compiled from the ontology (standard practice in structured generation), and the semantic layer is a LogitsProcessor that maintains a dictionary and applies conditional masking at type-token positions. The "bitwise AND of two masks" composition is the trivial conjunction operation. The "enabling dependency" concept, while empirically demonstrated, is architecturally unsurprising—of course a semantic lookup requires valid vocabulary to function. This reads more as a well-executed engineering integration than a research contribution at the level expected for a top venue.

- **DocRED results substantially weaken the headline claim.** The 46% DR reduction on DocRED (19.0% to 10.19%) is a far cry from "near-complete" elimination. While the paper correctly contextualizes this via constraint tightness, the title "Near-Complete Type-Valid Information Extraction" is misleading when applied to the more realistic, complex ontology. On DocRED, 33% of relation types still have >2% violation rates, and residual violations remain above 10%—this is not "near-complete" by any reasonable standard. The paper effectively demonstrates near-complete elimination only on a toy-scale ontology (7 relations).

- **The CF violation trade-off is severe and inadequately resolved.** CF rises from 0.08% to 9.9% on SciERC (Table 3). This means the system trades one class of ontological inconsistency for another. While the paper argues DR violations are "hard" (structurally invalid) and CF violations are "soft" (individual triples remain valid), downstream KG consumers that perform entity-centric reasoning will be severely impacted by inconsistent entity typing. The DR:CF ratio of approximately 1.5:1 on SciERC (14.4pp DR reduction vs. 9.8pp CF increase) means a substantial fraction of the "fix" is offset by a new problem. The paper acknowledges this but offers no mitigation beyond future work.

- **Extremely low absolute F1 raises validity concerns.** Relation F1 of ~8% is far below meaningful extraction quality. At this performance level, the model is extracting mostly noise, and "F1-neutral" constraint enforcement on noise-level extraction has limited practical significance. While the paper argues this is a zero-shot setting and F1 is a control variable, reviewers will legitimately question whether the violation patterns and enforcement dynamics observed at 8% F1 transfer to systems operating at 40-50% F1 (supervised SOTA). The constraint-tightness correlation, the enabling dependency ratio, and the CF trade-off severity could all change substantially at higher extraction quality.

- **Only 2 datasets, 2 models, zero-shot only.** The experimental scope is narrow for a systems/methods paper. SciERC (7 relations, 6 entity types) is a toy ontology; DocRED (96 relations, 6 entity types) has more relations but the same small entity type set. No biomedical or legal ontologies are tested despite the introduction's motivation citing these domains. No fine-tuned model experiments are reported, yet fine-tuned models are the practical deployment scenario. The cross-model validation covers only SciERC.

- **The tightness-violation correlation, while interesting, has limited predictive value.** Spearman rho=0.52 (p<0.001) explains roughly 27% of variance. The paper frames this as enabling "a priori estimates of constraint effectiveness," but a correlation that explains a quarter of the variance is a weak predictor, not a practical planning tool.

---

## 4. Novelty Assessment

The novelty of this work is modest. The two-layer architecture is conceptually straightforward: layer 1 is off-the-shelf XGrammar applied to an auto-generated JSON schema; layer 2 is a custom LogitsProcessor that maintains a name-to-type dictionary and masks logits at type-token positions based on domain/range lookups. The composition mechanism (bitwise AND) is trivial. The "enabling dependency" concept—that the semantic layer requires grammar-enforced vocabulary validity to function—is architecturally obvious once stated, though the empirical quantification (3.88x enabling ratio) adds some value.

The paper's closest mechanistic analog, acknowledged in Section 6, is type-constrained code generation (PLDI 2025), which compiles full type systems into prefix automata for logit masking. OntoCoDec applies essentially the same "type system -> automaton -> logit mask" pipeline to a simpler type system (flat domain/range sets vs. parametric polymorphism with subtyping). The paper argues the key difference is free-text entity type inference requiring a stateful registry, which is a valid distinction but a modest one—it amounts to maintaining a dictionary populated during generation.

The violation landscape study (Section 3) is the most novel contribution. No prior work has systematically measured ontology constraint violation rates across IE benchmarks, characterized their per-relation distribution, or demonstrated the prompt insufficiency phenomenon (particularly the Evaluate-for regression). The constraint tightness formalization and its correlation with violation rates, while simple, provide a useful analytical lens.

The "no prior work systematically measures or addresses ontology constraint violations" claim in Section 6 is defensible for the specific formulation (per-triple DR/RV/ET/CF violation taxonomy with systematic measurement), though post-hoc ontology validation systems (SPIRES, OntoLogX, ODKE+) implicitly measure violations as part of their correction pipelines. The claim could be more precisely stated as "no prior work systematically measures violation rates as a function of ontology constraint structure."

Overall, the novelty is below the threshold for a top venue. The engineering is competent, but the intellectual contribution—applying known constrained decoding techniques to IE with a straightforward stateful extension—does not advance the field's understanding of constrained generation in a fundamental way.

---

## 5. Related Work Gaps

The related work section is comprehensive but has several notable omissions:

- **REBEL (Cabot & Navigli, 2021)** — End-to-end relation extraction via seq2seq with constrained decoding over a linearized triple format. Directly relevant as a prior system that applies constrained decoding to RE, though at the vocabulary level only.

- **DeepStruct (Wang et al., 2022)** — Pre-trained on 28 datasets with structured output, relevant to the training-based paradigm discussion.

- **TANL (Paolini et al., 2021)** — Translation between augmented natural languages for structured prediction; pioneered the linearized triple format that this paper's JSON output extends.

- **SynCode (Ugare et al., 2024)** — Grammar-augmented LLM generation with incremental parsing, directly relevant to Section 6's grammar-constrained decoding paragraph. Claims faster and more general grammar enforcement than some cited systems.

- **SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024)** — Mentioned in Section 2.2 but not discussed in related work Section 6. Should be included in the grammar-constrained decoding paragraph for completeness.

- **Guidance (Microsoft)** — A widely-used constrained generation library that supports stateful constraints. Not cited anywhere despite being a practical competitor/alternative.

- **Post-hoc type checking in KG completion** — The KG completion literature has extensive work on type-constrained link prediction (e.g., TransE variants with type constraints, type-aware negative sampling). While not identical to IE, the constraint enforcement motivation overlaps.

- **PICARD (Scholak et al., 2021)** — Incremental parsing for constrained decoding in text-to-SQL. This is a close methodological precursor: it applies incremental validity checking during autoregressive generation, rejecting token candidates that would lead to invalid SQL. The semantic validity checking mechanism (parse the partial output, check against schema) is analogous to OntoCoDec's semantic layer. Its omission is surprising.

The paper would benefit from a paragraph explicitly contrasting with PICARD, as both systems perform incremental semantic validity checking during autoregressive generation against a schema, differing primarily in the constraint language (SQL grammar + database schema vs. IE ontology domain/range rules).

---

## 6. Questions for Authors

1. **CF trade-off quantification**: What is the net effect on downstream KG quality when DR decreases by 14.4pp but CF increases by 9.8pp? Have you measured any downstream task (e.g., question answering over the extracted KG) to assess whether the trade-off is net positive?

2. **F1 regime sensitivity**: Have you run any experiments with a fine-tuned model where F1 is in the 30-50% range? The violation dynamics could be qualitatively different when the model is extracting meaningful triples rather than noise.

3. **DocRED "near-complete" framing**: Given the 46% DR reduction on DocRED (10.19% residual), do you consider the title appropriate? Would "OntoCoDec: Type-Valid Information Extraction via Compiled Ontology Constraints" without "Near-Complete" be more honest?

4. **PICARD comparison**: How does OntoCoDec's semantic layer differ mechanistically from PICARD's incremental parsing approach? Both maintain generation state and validate against a schema during decoding.

5. **Graceful degradation frequency**: The paper mentions 1/998 DocRED docs trigger the grammar-first fallback. What is the per-triple fallback rate? Does this concentrate on specific relation types?

6. **Constraint tightness as a design guide**: Given rho=0.52, what actionable guidance does the tightness metric provide? Can ontology designers use it to predict whether OntoCoDec will be effective for their schema before running experiments?

7. **Why not a global entity registry?** The CF problem arises from per-relation independent type enforcement. A straightforward mitigation would be a global entity-type consensus mechanism (majority vote or first-assignment-wins). Was this attempted and found inadequate, or simply not explored?

---

## 7. Minor Issues

- The abstract contains `\placeholder{DocRED results.}` — incomplete.
- Section 7 conclusion contains `\placeholder{DocRED DR result...}` — incomplete.
- Table 4 (cross-dataset) has "TBD" for DocRED S1 results — incomplete for submission.
- The `.bib` entry for `synchromesh_neurips2022` has an incorrect venue in the cite key (NeurIPS vs. actual ICLR 2022); while the entry itself is correct, this may cause confusion.
- The `.bib` entry for `roth_yih_2004` cite key suggests AAAI but actual venue is CoNLL 2004 — same issue.
- Section 6 cites `zhou2026snowballing` with a comment "PENDING AUDIT: may need replacement" — this should be resolved before submission.
- The paper uses both `\sigma(r)` (Section 2) and `dom(r)/range(r)` (Section 4) for the domain/range mapping — notation should be unified.
- Relation F1 reported as "8.36" and "8.23" throughout — these should be explicitly stated as percentages (8.36%) to avoid ambiguity, as some readers may interpret them as absolute scores on a different scale.

---

## 8. Overall Score and Confidence

**Score: 3 (Weak Reject)**

**Confidence: 4 (High)**

**Justification**: The paper addresses a real problem (ontology constraint violations in LLM-based IE) and the violation landscape study is a genuine empirical contribution. However, the core technical contribution—applying XGrammar + a stateful logit mask processor—is an engineering integration of known techniques rather than a research advance. The "near-complete" headline claim is justified only on a toy-scale ontology (SciERC, 7 relations); on the more realistic DocRED (96 relations), the system achieves only 46% reduction with 10% residual violations. The CF trade-off (0.08% to 9.9%) partially offsets the DR gains. The extremely low absolute F1 (~8%) raises concerns about whether findings transfer to practical extraction systems. The experimental scope (2 datasets, 2 models, zero-shot only) is narrow for a methods paper.

For a top venue at 25% acceptance rate, I expect either (a) a more fundamental algorithmic contribution, (b) stronger empirical results across diverse settings, or (c) deeper theoretical insight. This paper provides competent engineering with a useful empirical study, but falls short on all three axes. The violation landscape study alone, while valuable, is insufficient to carry the paper.

**Recommendation**: The paper would be strengthened by (1) demonstrating effectiveness with fine-tuned models at meaningful F1 levels, (2) resolving or substantially mitigating the CF trade-off, (3) testing on ontologies with larger entity type sets (both SciERC and DocRED have only 6 entity types), and (4) more carefully scoping the "near-complete" claim to contexts where it is empirically justified.
